en: Khan Sary died first among the khans,
The shepherd of the people of Sandyrga;
All the heroes died.
When word of his heroism was heard,
The khan of Beijing was stirred to action.
“He never stood watching when battle began;
He is calamity itself,”
And the people of Chinmachin wept.
Told to take a cap, he took a head;
Told to spill blood, he spilled souls;
Told to drink water, he drank poison.
That dread calamity, Külchoro,
Was my lion’s confidant,
Your magnanimous father’s companion;
Their sheep shared one fold,
Their feasts shared one fellowship,
And all they found and gathered they held in common.
With your lionhearted father
He shared death and the same faith.
Yesterday at Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
When the massed Kyrgyz descended to the plain
And grappled in battle,
When dawn whitened over the mountains
And day was breaking,
Among the renowned Kyrgyz of Talas—
While he stood as their khan—
These words are not spoken in vain:
He was your lion father’s retainer,
The iron-covered gate of his enclosure,
The comrade of your leopard father,
The dashing warrior on the blaze-faced steed,
The mighty and renowned falcon.
Those who challenged him he set straight,
Those he speared numbered a thousand.
He guarded all that was precious,
Seized the crooked and made it straight.
He was that famed strength, that very bastion,
That lion surpassing mortal men,
The champion who humbled the arrogant.
His laughter ushered in the dawn;
He was the lion who humbled the arrogant.
A solid hammer of cave-forged steel
Is this Külchoro standing here.
If your gray-maned warrior father
Sent him ahead, the road opened fair;
If he led them, hosts followed behind.
His stature towers like a lofty mountain;
He is the thunderbolt that shattered the khagan.
Even death cannot disperse
Your uncle Külchoro’s ardor.
He is the strength with which you gird your waist,
The stronghold in which you lie secure;
He breaks through dead ends and opens roads.
This dark, sharp blade with the mottled hilt
Is the refuge beneath which the people dwell,
The sheltering, cliff-like mountain pass,
The lion who guards the nation.
He is an inheritance left by your father,
A peerless one proven before the people;
Among all the peoples of the world,
He is a peerless kinsman, tried and true.
Your elder brother was born of a khan
And brought turmoil upon the enemy.
He became a fortress built for Talas,
And the enemy who opposed him found the grave.
He drove the khagan’s people to the frontier.
When the Chinese armored themselves in stone,
Saying, “We shall seize Talas,”
Their finest warriors burned.
He hacked down all who encountered him,
Devoured all whom he met,
Cut down whoever crossed his path,
And ruined whoever faced him.
Such is the story of Külchoro.
Against the infidels swarming like black beetles,
He began a savage battle
And slew with his own hand
Their khan and elder, Kongurbay.
While your warrior father and khan still lived,
His prowess and lionhearted strength,
His valor surpassing multitudes—
Whenever he faced a challenging foe,
He surged like a lion.
His singular face shone brightly;
He girded on a silver belt,
And the thundering falcon’s
Face beamed with sunlight.
He girded on a golden belt,
And the poor, far-striding falcon’s
Face shone with moonlight.
When you beheld the falcon warrior,
He had filled out like a spring-fed lake;
His imposing bearing,
His face of many moods,
Had become as it was before.
Such is Külchoro’s nature:
His worth sets him apart from other men;
Let alone the Jediger, he possesses the might
To crush the whole age.
When Külchoro saw his sister-in-law,
He rejoiced and took heart.
He donned his arrow-proof coat,
Prepared all his weapons,
And belted on his unsheathed sword.
Like a cloud about to rain again,
His wrath spread over his face.
Thick-wristed, stone-hearted,
An imposing giant built like an elephant,
Your falcon, it seems, had come to full strength
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön,
And was about to unleash a great calamity.
Unable to depart from the black ridge,
How could he stand without avenging himself
By spilling blood and severing heads?
Never sated though he drank blood,
He bore the aspect of a wrestler;
Broad-chested and wide-breasted,
He bore the aspect of an avenger.
He looked ready to strike down
Whoever confronted him, like a wild boar.
He looked ready to subdue
And capture all he encountered.
To all his beleaguered people,
He was a mighty support, great as a mountain.
Your primal ancestor was Tügöl Khan,
And a holy man bestowed his blessing upon you;
This Külchoro standing here—
Consider him your father, my son.
He is that boundless, towering mountain pass;
If you enter among the enemy, he is your counsel,
If you enter the fire, he is your ember,
If you seek wisdom, he is your stratagem,
If you enter combat, he is your spear—
He is the lion who will stand firm for you.
He teaches what is unknown,
That wise, mace-wielding elephant.
When you enter battle, he is your helmet;
When you charge against the enemy,
He is your spear, stout-shafted and sharp-tipped;
When you stoop to strike the foe,
He is your mace from Emil.
If you train him well, none like him can be found;
He is your falcon, a keen goshawk.
If you receive him, he will be your stronghold;
Be sure to take him to yourself.”
His mother Chürök began before Seytek
To raise the clamor,
And began to stir
An incurable calamity.
While Aichürök was still speaking,
Before she had finished her words,
Divinely guarded Külchoro
Prepared as though to flee.
Inspiration came to him from the unseen;
He stiffened like cured leather,
His shovel-like teeth gleaming white.
The blazing fire within him was boundless,
Its like had never been born;
He was a tempest sprung from mankind,
And no such man existed among warriors.
He pranced sideways like a racehorse,
And began to speak with laughter,
Gleaming in his mail coat.
Külchoro, fairer than any man,
From the pavilion with golden pillars
Toward his sister-in-law, a woman like the moon,
Came walking softly.
Aichürök was his sister-in-law,
Yet more than that, his mother;
She had come when he was tiny,
And he had clung to her in a mother’s stead,
For she had fed him doe’s milk.
To the sister-in-law he regarded as his mother,
Choro approached and said:
“Sister, it is truly the Jediger whom I face,
And valiant Kyyaz with whom I contend.
Your Külchoro is like hardened red iron;
Let no one say he met a true slaughter
And perished there.
I was your renowned brother-in-law,
And you were my heroic sister-in-law.
Have you a coat for me to wear?
Let me proudly don your coat;
The one I must confront is valiant Kyyaz.
I shall face him once and see;
If fate has come, I shall die.
I shall behold the unyielding truth
That the Creator has inscribed for me.
If death comes and my days are done,
Do not grieve for a servant like me.
If I should die,
I was a son worth no more than dogskin;
If I survive,
I am a servant worth no more than sheepskin.
How could I be one who girded his waist firmly,
One born of the same blood as the falcon,
Sprung from the pure loins
Of Manas, radiant as the moon?
How could I have burst forth, tearing
The womb of my poor mother Kanykey?
When was I ever a son of Manas?
If my strength fails and power leaves me,
I shall die at the hands of valiant Kyyaz;
He looks ready to strike.
He rages like a tiger,
And none who clash with him survive.
His movement is like a gathering storm,
His countenance like a snowy mountainside,
His menace like a deep abyss;
Let alone the Jediger, if he is roused,
He seems able to swallow the world.
He rages like a tiger,
And none who fight him survive.
When he opens his cavernous mouth,
The cold blast issuing from it
Is like the wind along a mountain ridge.
The broad expanse of his two cheeks
Is like a vast blue field spread wide.
Your dark-browed Külchoro
Looks ready to devour all who confront him.
His upturned mustache
Is like a saber from Bukhara.
The icy glare of his two eyes
Is like flame burning upon a highland.
The narrow bridge of his nose
Is like a saber’s sheath.
When you look into his eye sockets,
They resemble the bed of a dried-up river.
The fierce, dark-browed warrior
Looks ready to drain whoever meets him.
The heroic Choro’s imposing form
Seems able to turn a mighty river.
If his stubborn fury seizes him,
He will unleash a grievous disaster;
If he comes within reach of Kyyaz,
He will seize him and dash him to the ground.
Not valiant Kyyaz alone—
Though the Jediger swarm in countless hosts,
He will slaughter them without leaving a hair.
When the falcon stirs,
Would the whole world dare confront him?
If all creation attacked in fury,
Could any man defeat Choro?
My valiant prince was lost,
My two knees buckled,
My suffering soul was overcome,
My tiny life cried out,
My whole body quaked
When I was caught in a net
That no leap could break.
My two hands were bound,
My two eyes stared wide,
When I fell captive.
When the seething Jediger host
Closed in and reached me,
They were thousands, and I alone,
